vocabulary.definition: A mathematical statement you believe is true but have not yet proven.

vocabulary.definition: A single example that shows a statement is not always true.

revealWordProblem.title: Apply: Another Option for the Community Garden
revealWordProblem.text:
Another design for the community garden bed, shown here, is also being considered. Both designs are built from rectangular boxes with the same depth.
Question: Which garden bed design would you recommend, and why?
revealWordProblem.imageAlt: Two labeled garden-bed designs built from rectangular boxes, with side lengths marked in feet.
revealWordProblem.sampleAnswer: I broke each design into rectangular boxes, used the labeled lengths to find the area (or volume) of each box, and added the parts to get a total for each design. Then I compared the totals and recommended the design with more planting space for the same depth. I named the numbers I compared so my recommendation is backed by the measurements, not just by how the design looks.

questions.stem: An egg muffin is about 60 calories. A plate holds 4 egg muffins. About how many calories are on the plate?
questions.explanation: 4 muffins at about 60 calories each is 60 × 4 = 240 calories.
choiceFeedback: That divides 60 by 4 instead of multiplying.
That adds 60 + 4 instead of multiplying.
That multiplies 60 by 10 instead of by 4.
hints: How many muffins, and how many calories in each one?
4 equal groups of 60.
Multiply 60 × 4.
questions.stemEs: Un panecillo de huevo tiene unas 60 calorías. Un plato lleva 4 panecillos de huevo. ¿Aproximadamente cuántas calorías hay en el plato?
questions.explanationEs: 4 panecillos de unas 60 calorías cada uno es 60 × 4 = 240 calorías.
hintsEs: ¿Cuántos panecillos, y cuántas calorías tiene cada uno?
4 grupos iguales de 60.
Multiplica 60 × 4.

questions.stem: A large cereal box is 8 in long, 3 in wide, and 10 in tall. What is its volume?
questions.explanation: Volume of a rectangular prism is length × width × height: 8 × 3 × 10 = 240 cubic inches.
choiceFeedback: That adds 8 + 3 + 10 instead of multiplying the dimensions.
That multiplies only 8 × 10 and leaves out the 3-inch width.
The number is right, but volume is measured in CUBIC inches — square inches measure area.
hints: Volume of a box is length × width × height.
Multiply 8 × 3 first, then use the height.
questions.stemEs: Una caja grande de cereal mide 8 pulgadas de largo, 3 de ancho y 10 de alto. ¿Cuál es su volumen?
questions.explanationEs: El volumen de un prisma rectangular es largo × ancho × alto: 8 × 3 × 10 = 240 pulgadas cúbicas.
hintsEs: El volumen de una caja es largo × ancho × alto.
Multiplica primero 8 × 3 y luego usa la altura.

questions.stem: Each jumbo box holds 400 cubic inches. How much do TWO jumbo boxes hold?
questions.explanation: Two boxes of 400 cubic inches each is 400 × 2 = 800 cubic inches.
choiceFeedback: That divides 400 by 2 instead of doubling.
That adds 400 + 2 instead of doubling.
That multiplies 400 by 10 instead of by 2.
hints: Two equal boxes — what operation combines them?
Double 400.
questions.stemEs: Cada caja jumbo contiene 400 pulgadas cúbicas. ¿Cuánto contienen DOS cajas jumbo?
questions.explanationEs: Dos cajas de 400 pulgadas cúbicas cada una son 400 × 2 = 800 pulgadas cúbicas.
hintsEs: Dos cajas iguales — ¿qué operación las combina?
Duplica 400.

level2.stem: Three large boxes hold 240 cubic inches each. Two jumbo boxes hold 400 cubic inches each. Which is the correct volume comparison?
choices: 240 cubic inches vs. 400 cubic inches — the jumbo option holds more
480 cubic inches vs. 800 cubic inches — the jumbo option holds more
720 cubic inches vs. 800 cubic inches — the jumbo option holds more
720 cubic inches vs. 800 cubic inches — the large option holds more
level2.explanation: 240 × 3 = 720 and 400 × 2 = 800; since 800 > 720, the two jumbo boxes hold more in total.
choiceFeedback: That compares one box of each size instead of the full purchase — three larges vs. two jumbos.
480 comes from 240 × 2 — the large option has THREE boxes, not two.
The totals are right, but 800 is GREATER than 720, so the jumbo option wins the comparison.
hints: Find each TOTAL before comparing.
Which total is greater?
level2.stemEs: Tres cajas grandes contienen 240 pulgadas cúbicas cada una. Dos cajas jumbo contienen 400 pulgadas cúbicas cada una. ¿Cuál es la comparación correcta de volumen?
level2.explanationEs: 240 × 3 = 720 y 400 × 2 = 800; como 800 > 720, las dos cajas jumbo contienen más en total.
hintsEs: Halla cada TOTAL antes de comparar.
¿Cuál total es mayor?

level2.stem: One garden bed is 4 ft long, 3 ft wide, and 2 ft deep. A second bed is 6 ft long, 2 ft wide, and 2 ft deep. How much soil fills BOTH beds?
level2.explanation: First bed: 4 × 3 × 2 = 24 cubic feet. Second bed: 6 × 2 × 2 = 24 cubic feet. Together: 24 + 24 = 48 cubic feet.
choiceFeedback: That adds all the dimensions (4+3+2+6+2+2) instead of multiplying within each bed.
24 cubic feet is only ONE bed — the problem asks for both.
That multiplies the two bed volumes (24 × ... ) too far — you ADD the volumes of the parts, you don't double the total.
hints: Find each bed's volume separately, then combine.
Add the two volumes.
level2.stemEs: Un cantero mide 4 pies de largo, 3 de ancho y 2 de profundidad. Un segundo cantero mide 6 pies de largo, 2 de ancho y 2 de profundidad. ¿Cuánta tierra llena AMBOS canteros?
level2.explanationEs: Primer cantero: 4 × 3 × 2 = 24 pies cúbicos. Segundo cantero: 6 × 2 × 2 = 24 pies cúbicos. Juntos: 24 + 24 = 48 pies cúbicos.
hintsEs: Halla el volumen de cada cantero por separado y luego combínalos.
Suma los dos volúmenes.

level2.stem: The group found the volume by decomposing the garden into prisms and adding. Why would they compute it a SECOND, different way?
choices: Because the first way is always wrong
To get a bigger number for the soil order
If both ways give the same answer, the solution is accurate
Because volume changes each time you measure it
level2.explanation: The book models exactly this: two different decompositions both gave 48 cubic feet, so the solutions match and the answer is accurate.
choiceFeedback: The first way can be perfectly correct — the second way CONFIRMS it rather than replaces it.
Checking is about accuracy, not inflating the answer — both ways should give the SAME number.
The garden's volume is fixed — what could vary is our calculation, which is why we check it.
hints: What did the two solutions in the lesson have in common?
The solutions were the same for both ways.
Matching answers mean the calculation is accurate.
level2.stemEs: El grupo halló el volumen descomponiendo el jardín en prismas y sumando. ¿Por qué lo calcularían una SEGUNDA vez de otra manera?
level2.explanationEs: El libro modela exactamente esto: dos descomposiciones distintas dieron 48 pies cúbicos, así que las soluciones coinciden y la respuesta es correcta.
hintsEs: ¿Qué tenían en común las dos soluciones de la lección?
Las soluciones fueron las mismas por los dos caminos.
Respuestas que coinciden significan que el cálculo es correcto.

level3.stem: A student claims: “Greater box volume ALWAYS means more cereal inside.” Which is the best counterexample?
choices: A large box that costs more than a jumbo box
A jumbo box with more volume that is sold half-filled with air
Two jumbo boxes that are easier to store than three large boxes
A box of a different cereal brand
level3.explanation: A counterexample must break the claim itself: a bigger box holding less cereal (more air) shows greater volume does not guarantee more cereal.
choiceFeedback: Price does not test the claim — the claim links volume to AMOUNT of cereal, not cost.
Storage convenience is a different argument entirely; it says nothing about how much cereal is inside.
Changing the brand changes the product, but does not show a bigger box holding less cereal.
hints: A counterexample must make the claim FALSE in one case.
The claim connects volume to amount of cereal.
Find the case where volume is bigger but cereal is not.
level3.stemEs: Un estudiante afirma: “Más volumen de caja SIEMPRE significa más cereal adentro.” ¿Cuál es el mejor contraejemplo?
level3.explanationEs: Un contraejemplo debe romper la afirmación misma: una caja más grande que contiene menos cereal (más aire) muestra que más volumen no garantiza más cereal.
hintsEs: Un contraejemplo debe hacer FALSA la afirmación en un caso.
La afirmación conecta el volumen con la cantidad de cereal.
Halla el caso donde el volumen es mayor pero el cereal no.

level3.stem: The garden needs 48 cubic feet of soil. One decomposition used two prisms of 24 cubic feet each. Which of these is ANOTHER decomposition of the same garden volume?
level3.explanation: 4 × 4 × 2 = 32 and 4 × 2 × 2 = 16, and 32 + 16 = 48 cubic feet — the same total by a different split.
choiceFeedback: 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 and 3 × 3 × 2 = 18 give 45 cubic feet, not 48.
4 × 4 × 2 = 32 twice gives 64 cubic feet, not 48.
6 × 4 × 2 = 48 and 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 give 56 cubic feet, not 48.
hints: Compute each prism's volume, then add.
The parts must total exactly 48.
level3.stemEs: El jardín necesita 48 pies cúbicos de tierra. Una descomposición usó dos prismas de 24 pies cúbicos cada uno. ¿Cuál de estas es OTRA descomposición del mismo volumen del jardín?
level3.explanationEs: 4 × 4 × 2 = 32 y 4 × 2 × 2 = 16, y 32 + 16 = 48 pies cúbicos — el mismo total con una división distinta.
hintsEs: Calcula el volumen de cada prisma y luego suma.
Las partes deben sumar exactamente 48.

level3.stem: Another garden bed design is also being considered. What information would you need to compare the two designs, and how would you argue for the one you recommend?
level3.modelAnswer: I would need the dimensions of each design so I could compute both volumes in cubic feet. Then I would build my argument with equations — the volumes — and with words, like which design fits the space better or is easier to reach. I would state my recommendation and defend it with both kinds of evidence.
